identity.manufacturer_reference: Mercedes-Benz OM 471.9, power code M3D (engine series 471.9 in model 963/964)
identity.disclaimer: Public-spec reference simulation built from published service-literature figures. Not an OEM calibration, not a digital twin, and not endorsed by Mercedes-Benz. Manufacturer and engine names are used as factual references only. Values marked calibrated are our estimates, not OEM data. The engine speeds at which this model reaches the published 375 kW and 2500 Nm are an outcome of our calibration; the manual does not publish them.

provenance.value_note: 35 degrees of crank between shut and full lift, the same as the exhaust side. The manual publishes no valve lift profile for either.
provenance.purpose: Sets how quickly the intake port opens and shuts. Its acoustic job is the opposite of the exhaust ramp's: the exhaust ramp has to be short so blowdown stays a sharp pulse, while this one has to be long enough that trapping the charge does not put a fast edge into the cylinder pressure trace, which the structural path would differentiate into an impulse. A finite ramp is the whole reason the intake side stopped stepping in milestone 12.

provenance.value_note: 2.5e-3 m^2 for both intake valves at full lift, matching the exhaust port area. The manual publishes the valve count but no lift profile or flow area for either side.
provenance.purpose: Sets how much air the cylinder actually traps, which is what the smoke limit reads and so what the fuelled peaks are calibrated against. It replaces air_path.volumetric_efficiency as the knob on trapping: with a real port the trapping efficiency is an outcome of area, speed and manifold pressure rather than a fixed multiplier, so it falls with engine speed on its own.

provenance.value_note: 35 degrees of crank between shut and full lift. The manual publishes no valve lift profile.
provenance.purpose: Sets how sharply blowdown starts. A slow ramp leaves the port nearly shut at peak pressure difference, which makes the exhaust pulse a smooth hump with no harmonic content and no audible sound.

provenance.value_note: 2.5e-3 m^2 for both exhaust valves at full lift. The manual publishes the valve count but no lift profile or flow area.
provenance.purpose: Scales the exhaust blowdown that drives the acoustic source: a bigger port makes a louder pulse.

provenance.value_note: 0.02, so plus or minus 2% about nominal. No two exhaust ports in a real head flow identically: core shift in the casting, valve seat cut, and guide wear all differ cylinder to cylinder. The magnitude is a plausible build tolerance and nothing more; the source manual publishes no port areas at all, let alone their scatter.
provenance.purpose: Breaks the cylinder-to-cylinder symmetry of the exhaust pulse train. Six bit-identical cylinders sum to a mathematically pure harmonic comb with no jitter and no amplitude scatter, and the ear hears that as synthesised rather than as an engine. Drawn once per cylinder at reset from the reset seed, never per step, so determinism is exact. Deliberately far too small to move any calibration result: a spread that shifts peak power is not modelling a tolerance, and the validator caps it at 0.1 for that reason.

provenance.value_note: 0.00075 rad per mg, about 8 degrees of retard at full fuelling. The source manual does not publish this.

provenance.value_note: 0.015, so plus or minus 1.5% about the commanded quantity. Real injectors are matched to a tolerance, not to each other. The manual publishes the rail and amplified pressure limits and nothing about delivery scatter.
provenance.purpose: Gives each cylinder its own delivered fuel quantity for the same command, so the six burns differ slightly in heat release and therefore in pulse amplitude and in clatter. Companion to `valvetrain.exhaust_area_spread` and drawn on the same terms: once per cylinder at reset, from the reset seed. The smoke limit still applies after the trim, so a generous injector on a cylinder short of air is still held to the air it has.

provenance.value_note: 0.02, so plus or minus 2% about the commanded quantity for each cycle. Published measurements of coefficient of variation in indicated mean effective pressure for heavy-duty diesels run a few percent at light load and under one percent at high load; this value sits inside that range, and the load dependence is not scheduled - it emerges, because a lightly loaded cycle has a long ignition delay and a large premixed fraction, so the same wobble in fuel moves the pressure rise further. The source manual publishes nothing about combustion variability.
provenance.purpose: Gives each cycle its own delivered fuel quantity, so no two firing events are identical even from the same cylinder. The per-cylinder sibling gives each cylinder a fixed character; this is the other defect, and a different one. With build scatter alone every cycle of a given cylinder is bit-identical to its last and the output is a comb of infinitely narrow lines, which the ear hears as a synthesiser rather than as an engine. Real diesels run a few percent cycle-to-cycle variation in indicated work from injector shot-to-shot spread, residual mixing and turbulence, and that is what gives the firing orders their width. Drawn once per cylinder per cycle at intake valve closing from the reset seed, never per step, so determinism and batch invariance are untouched. The smoke limit still applies after the trim.

The source manual does not publish this.

provenance.value_note: 10 degrees of crank either side of the charging peak. The source manual does not publish this.

provenance.value_note: 10 degrees of crank either side of the release peak. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Duration of the release lobe. Narrow and late, so the cylinder is dumped at peak compression rather than part way up it. Widening this measurably lowers peak cylinder pressure below the motored trace, which contradicts the manual's 'the compression pressure is increased as a result'.

provenance.value_note: 0.1, so the wastegate loop runs at a tenth of its fuelled gains and slew rate while braking. The source manual does not publish this.

provenance.value_note: 560 rpm idle speed
provenance.locator: SN00.00-W-0002-05H, Technical data of diesel engine OM 471, printed page 11 (PDF page 14)

provenance.value_note: 1.2 mg per (rad/s) of speed error. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Proportional term of the idle governor. Requests fuel, never torque.

provenance.value_note: 0.6 mg per (rad/s) per second. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Integral term holding the published 560 rpm idle against friction and accessory load.

provenance.value_note: 40 mg integrator clamp.
provenance.purpose: Prevents integral windup while cranking, which would overshoot idle.

provenance.value_note: 1900 rpm. The manual publishes neither rated nor governed speed.
provenance.purpose: Speed at which fuelling starts being withdrawn.

provenance.value_note: 2100 rpm. The manual publishes neither rated nor governed speed.
provenance.purpose: Speed at which fuelling reaches zero.

provenance.value_note: 25 N m constant accessory drag. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Fan, alternator, compressor and pumps as an explicit resisting term.

provenance.value_note: 0.02 N m per (rad/s). The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Speed-dependent part of the accessory drag.

provenance.value_note: 5000 N m ceiling for the user-supplied and dynamometer load.
provenance.purpose: Bounds the external load input; driveline behaviour arrives in Milestone 4.

provenance.value_note: 24 V nominal system voltage
provenance.locator: Bosch parts catalogue entry for HEF109-M 24V, part number 0 001 330 050

provenance.value_note: 7.8 kW nominal power. This is a VALIDATION TARGET and not a solver input: nothing in the stepping path reads it, and starter_sweep measures whether the calibrated circuit below actually reaches it. The engine brake published anchors are handled the same way and for the same reason - a model permitted to read its own answer proves nothing.
provenance.locator: Bosch parts catalogue entry for HEF109-M 24V, part number 0 001 330 050

provenance.value_note: 12 teeth on the pinion
provenance.locator: Bosch parts catalogue entry for HEF109-M 24V, part number 0 001 330 050

provenance.value_note: 145 teeth. Neither source publishes this: the engine manual says nothing about the flywheel and the starter catalogue describes only the pinion. With 12 pinion teeth it gives a 12.08:1 reduction, which is inside the ordinary heavy-duty range, and it is the dominant lever on both the cranking speed and the mesh frequency the starter acoustic path whines at - 145 teeth puts the mesh at 483 Hz at 200 crank rpm.
provenance.purpose: Sets the reduction from pinion to crank, and with it both the crank torque available and the tooth-mesh rate that is the whole of the starter sound. The two cannot be separated, which is why the gear ratio is derived from the tooth counts rather than configured beside them.

provenance.value_note: 0.01263 ohm for the whole loop: battery internal resistance, cables, brushes and armature together. Gives 1900 A at stall, which is the right order for a 24 V heavy-duty starter, and pulls the terminals from 24 V to 9.9 V at cranking speed. The catalogue publishes no resistance and no current at all.
provenance.purpose: The single most important electrical value here. It sets stall current, and with it both the stall torque and how far the supply sags - and the sag is what makes a heavy diesel start audibly labour as each cylinder comes up on compression.

provenance.value_note: 9.9752e-5 N m per (ampere x ampere of field flux). Fitted, with the drag term below, so that mechanical output at the pinion shaft peaks at exactly the published 7.8 kW - which it does, at 149 crank rpm. The units are N m/A^2 rather than N m/A because a series machine makes its own field from its own armature current, so torque goes as the square of it until the iron saturates.
provenance.purpose: Torque per amp, and by the same constant the back-EMF per rad/s. It has to be one number in both places or the machine would generate or destroy energy: torque times speed and EMF times current are the same product written twice.

provenance.value_note: 620 A, the current at which field flux reaches half of its saturated value. Without saturation a series machine’s torque would go as the square of current for ever, and stall torque would come out several times what this machine can make. Iron gives up instead.
provenance.purpose: Bends the torque-current relation over, which is what makes the modelled stall torque physical rather than merely large.

provenance.value_note: 0.063 N m per (rad/s) of motor speed: armature windage and brush drag. It puts the no-load speed at 330 crank rpm, and it is load-bearing far out of proportion to its size.
provenance.purpose: This is what gives the machine a finite no-load speed. A series motor with no internal drag has none at all - it runs away as its load goes to zero - so without this the cranking speed would be set by whatever the engine happened to resist. With it, the cranking speed is an outcome of the two machines meeting rather than a number anybody chose.

provenance.value_note: 0.90 for the pinion-to-ring-gear mesh. The catalogue publishes nothing about it.
provenance.purpose: Losses between the pinion shaft and the crankshaft.

provenance.value_note: 8 ms for the pinion to seat in the ring gear. Fast enough to be a clunk rather than a swell, and about 320 solver steps, so the engagement is integrated rather than assigned.
provenance.purpose: The fast end of the engagement, and what a start clunks with. It is also what stops the torque arriving as a step: the two-field starter this replaced went from nothing to 1500 N m in a single 25 us step, and a step in a radiated quantity is an impulse.

provenance.value_note: 60 ms between the solenoid energising and the main contacts closing. The two-stage sequence itself is published for this starter family; the 60 ms is not.
provenance.purpose: Holds the main current off until the pinion is already in mesh. Releasing full current into a pinion that has not seated is what wears ring gears out, and the manufacturer describes the two-stage engagement as being for exactly that.

provenance.value_note: 420 rpm, above the cranking speed the model reaches and below the 560 rpm published idle target.
provenance.purpose: Where the start relay drops out, so a driver holding the key past the catch still gets a normal start. It is also the boundary between the cranking and running run states. That boundary used to be the old starter taper cut-out speed, which could not be moved without changing the torque as well - so run-state read running while the starter was still dragging the crank through a few hundred rpm, and loading an engine there very nearly stalls it.

provenance.value_note: 0.15 of a tooth pitch for one tooth to come into contact. Nothing about the mesh is published.
provenance.purpose: The acoustic counterpart of a valve ramp width, and it matters for the same reason. Spread the contact across the whole pitch and the mesh force is a smooth hum with essentially no harmonic content, which is not what a starter sounds like; a tooth meshes quickly and the whine is buzzy. Narrow it much further and the contact is a bare impulse landing on a handful of solver steps.

provenance.value_note: 0.12. The clunk, against the running mesh. It needs a number of its own because the two halves of the starter sound are normalised against different things: the mesh drive is transmitted torque over stall torque and runs at about 0.12 while cranking, and this term is the derivative of a ramp and arrives at pi/2. Unscaled the engagement is roughly thirteen times the whine, which a listener heard as a short bark with no machine behind it. Physically it should be the smaller of the two anyway - at first contact the crank is stationary and the main contacts have not closed, so the pinion slides into mesh barely turning and there is very little energy in the impact. At 0.18 the clunk still dominated enough to pull the path loudest octave down to 205 Hz; at 0.12 the loudest octave is 433 Hz, which is the mesh.
provenance.purpose: Sets how prominent the engagement and disengagement impacts are against the continuous whine. Zero is meaningful and gives a starter that fades in silently; too high and the start is a bark with no machine behind it, which is the defect this value was introduced to fix.

provenance.value_note: 3.5 kg m^2 for crankshaft, flywheel and rotating accessories. The manual publishes NO rotating inertia, and the published complete-engine mass is deliberately not used here.
provenance.purpose: Sets crank acceleration for a given net torque.

provenance.value_note: approx. 1200 kg complete-engine weight. Metadata only: never used as flywheel or rotating inertia.
provenance.locator: SN00.00-W-0002-05H, Technical data of diesel engine OM 471, printed page 11 (PDF page 14)

provenance.value_note: combustion pressures of up to 230 bar; used here as a validation and safety envelope, not as a pressure target
provenance.locator: SN00.00-W-0002-04H, Engine OM 471, printed page 10 (PDF page 13)

provenance.value_note: 2400 rpm hard numerical guard, above the governed cut-out.
provenance.purpose: Rejects a diverged solution rather than letting crank speed run away.

provenance.value_note: 3000 K hard numerical guard.
provenance.purpose: Rejects a diverged single-zone gas state.

provenance.value_note: 25 microseconds, about 0.36 degrees of crank rotation at 2400 rpm.
provenance.purpose: Fixed integration step, small enough that the explicit crank and gas integration stays stable across the whole speed range.

provenance.value_note: 20000 steps, i.e. 0.5 s of simulated time per advance call.
provenance.purpose: Keeps the WASM boundary coarse while bounding the work of a single call.

provenance.value_note: 3.5 m. Not published, and it drives an audible resonance, so it is exactly the kind of value that has to be declared rather than assumed. Plausible for a tractor unit with a vertical stack; the manual gives no exhaust geometry whatsoever.
provenance.purpose: Sets the pipe resonance together with the speed of sound: the quarter-wave sits at c / 4L and the odd harmonics above it land among the firing orders, which is what gives the exhaust a pitch of its own independent of engine speed. Longer is deeper. Both duct delay buffers are sized from this at construction.

provenance.value_note: 0.008 m^2, about a 100 mm bore. Not published.
provenance.purpose: Cross-section of the duct. The aftertreatment box is a compliance, and a compliance behaves like an added duct length of volume over area, so without an area the box cannot say what it does to the pipe. Larger area means the same box lengthens the duct less.

provenance.value_note: -0.8. Not published, and not measurable from anything the manual contains. A real unflanged pipe mouth returns nearly all of a 200 Hz wave, so the damping a truck exhaust has belongs to the aftertreatment substrate and not here; using this to quiet the duct would misattribute it.
provenance.purpose: Reflection coefficient at the pipe mouth. Negative because an open end is a pressure node and inverts the wave. Its magnitude is how much of each pulse is returned to form a standing wave rather than radiated away, and it also sets how much reaches a listener: what radiates is the mouth's volume velocity, which goes as 1 - R, so a harder end is a stronger velocity antinode and a louder pipe. Together with the manifold reflection and the substrate transmission it forms the waveguide's loop gain, and validation requires it to stay inside (-1, 0) or the duct is unstable.

provenance.value_note: 2000 Hz. Not published.
provenance.purpose: One-pole loss on the reflected wave, standing for the fact that a pipe mouth radiates poorly at low frequency and well high up. It is why a real pipe's low resonances are sharp and its high ones are damped. Lower values damp the pipe more and make the note duller and shorter.

provenance.value_note: 0.012 m^3, twelve litres of free acoustic volume. The manual describes the DPF and SCR architecture at length and publishes no dimensions at all; this is the gas space, not the package size, and most of a real box is substrate rather than air.
provenance.purpose: The box is a compliance shunted on the duct, which at the wavelengths that set the first few resonances behaves like an extra length of volume over area. So it lowers the pipe's resonance rather than filtering it. The approximation is a low-frequency one and stops describing the box once a wavelength is comparable with the box's own dimensions; nothing in the audible exhaust note is up there.

provenance.value_note: 0.61, about -4.3 dB of wave amplitude per pass and -8.6 dB per round trip. The manual describes the DPF and SCR architecture at length and publishes no acoustic figure for it; wall-flow filters are commonly credited with insertion losses of order 10 to 15 dB, so this is a conservative reading of that.
provenance.purpose: Fraction of the wave surviving one traverse of the aftertreatment substrate, taken once each way and so twice per round trip. The volume above makes the box a compliance that lengthens the duct; this is the other half of what a box is, and it is where a real exhaust system's damping actually lives. A wall-flow filter forces the gas through porous ceramic, which is a flow resistance and therefore broadband, so it is a scalar rather than another corner frequency. One means a lossless box and leaves the duct damped only at its mouth: an organ pipe with a round-trip gain of 0.72 and a T60 near 360 ms, in which whichever firing order lands on a resonance swallows the rest of the note and the engine drones on one pitch. Lower values shorten the ring and spread the exhaust into a harmonic series; too low and the pipe has no note left at all.

provenance.value_note: 14 dB. Turbines are commonly quoted as giving order 10 to 20 dB; the manual gives no figure for this one.
provenance.purpose: Broadband attenuation across the turbine, applied above the corner below. Acoustically a turbine is a large silencer, and this is the term that makes the engine read as turbocharged rather than as open-piped. Too little and the exhaust is raw and sharp; too much and the exhaust note disappears behind the block noise.

provenance.value_note: 400 Hz. Not published.
provenance.purpose: Corner above which the turbine's insertion loss applies. Below it the pulse passes; above it the loss is taken. Moving it down mutes more of the pulse's edge and leaves more of its fundamental.

provenance.value_note: 0.10 m, the runner nearest the turbine on a log manifold. Not published.
provenance.purpose: Shortest exhaust manifold runner. With the longest it sets the spread of arrival times at the turbine, which is what makes an inline six sound like an inline six rather than like six identical pops - and what makes geometry.firing_order audible at all rather than merely validated.

provenance.value_note: 0.70 m, the runner furthest from the turbine. Not published.
provenance.purpose: Longest exhaust manifold runner. Given as a span with the minimum rather than a length per cylinder, so this section carries no cylinder count and a configuration with a different number of cylinders uses it unchanged. Validation requires it to exceed the minimum: a manifold whose runners are all one length cannot make the firing order audible.

provenance.value_note: 94 dB reference for the reported exhaust level. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Reference the level meter is quoted against. A display reference only: it is not a claim about how loud the real engine is.

provenance.value_note: 1.41, which is +3.0 dB. Introduced on a listening report that everything was too quiet, and separated from the four path gains deliberately: those say the balance and this says the level, and the level had to move without re-deriving four calibrations that are each about a ratio. Applied in common to all four paths it cannot change a band share, a comb share or the ratio between any two of them - and measurement confirms that, every band share below cruise being identical before and after. What it does change is where the limiter engages. +3.0 dB is the most a common raise can give before an acceptance criterion breaks: measured, idle rises the full 3 dB to a peak of 0.148 while cruise, full load, rated and brake are already on the 0.85 knee and gain about 1 dB, and rated-1800 crest falls from 9.3 to exactly 9.0 dB against a floor of 9. A raise of +4.5 dB reads 8.9 dB there and +6.0 dB reads 8.8, both failing.
provenance.purpose: How much of the operating range sits under the limiter knee. The engine spans about 22 dB from governed idle to rated, and the ceiling is necessarily set by the loud end, so the quiet end is quiet by construction; this decides how quiet. Too low and idle and a start are inaudible on ordinary hardware, which is the defect it was introduced to fix; too high and the limiter is working at every loaded point and pulse dynamics go with it, which is measurable as crest factor and is what bounds the value.

provenance.value_note: 26. The acoustic source is the net mass flow the exhaust port actually passed, in kg/s, taken from the same `flow::exchange` call that moves the gas rather than recomputed beside it. A mass flow in kg/s is of order one, so it needs a modest scaling rather than a large one. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Brings the radiated exhaust signal to a usable level before the soft clipper, and sets the exhaust against the block. Set so the loudest realistic condition - the start transient, which is louder than full load - approaches the knee without sitting on it. Driving it far past the knee flat-tops the waveform, and a flat-topped wave is full of high harmonics: an audible buzz, not a louder engine.

provenance.value_note: 20 Hz. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Removes the standing pressure offset so only the pulses remain, and keeps the signal from drifting off centre.

provenance.value_note: 0.85. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Ceiling the limiter holds the summed mix to, which is what guarantees samples stay inside [-1, 1] without hard clipping. The limiter reaches it by reducing gain rather than by reshaping the sample, so a signal held here keeps its pulse shape; the remaining headroom to full scale is a smooth shoulder that only an overshoot can reach.

provenance.value_note: 0.3 s. Chosen as a multiple of a firing period rather than by ear: the fastest firing rate in the range is 90 Hz at 1800 rpm and the slowest that limits at all is 65 Hz under brake, so 0.3 s is twenty periods and the gain recovers by about 5% between combustion events. Shorter and the follower starts tracking individual pulses, which is the per-sample waveshaping it was introduced to stop; much longer and a single loud transient ducks the engine for a second afterwards. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Time constant the limiter's gain recovers towards unity with. There is no matching attack parameter because attack is instantaneous: the gain drops to exactly what the ceiling requires on the sample that requires it, which is what bounds the output with no lookahead and no latency. Release is therefore the only choice, and it has to be long compared with a firing period, because a follower quick enough to recover between combustion events scales each pulse by a different amount and deforms the pulse train it is meant to be passing.

provenance.value_note: 0.20. Calibrated against the audio_probe band shares, with the ceiling set by the soft clipper rather than by taste: above roughly ten the summed signal lives on the knee at load and the saturation manufactures its own harmonics in the same band this path exists to supply. Halved from 0.40 in milestone 15, and not because the path was meant to get quieter: reshaping the mode weights changes how much drive energy the bank captures, so the level had to come down to leave the exhaust-over-block balance where it was. The weights say what the block sounds like and this says how loud it is; separating the two is what let the shape change without moving the balance. The source manual does not publish this.
provenance.purpose: Sets the level of the structural radiation path against the exhaust path. The structural path is combustion noise: the premixed pressure rise ringing the block, head and covers, which is what makes a diesel identifiable as one rather than as a generic engine. Too low and the engine is a low-frequency drone; too high and the clatter buries the firing orders and drives the sum into the soft-clip knee, where saturation invents harmonics in the band being measured and the improvement becomes an artefact of clipping rather than of the model.

provenance.value_note: Six modes at 210, 380, 750, 1400, 2400 and 3600 Hz with Q of 9, 10, 7, 8, 13 and 14, weighted 1.15, 1.3, 2.2, 1.5, 2.0 and 2.5. Plausible for the block, head and covers of an engine of this size and nothing more than that; the source manual publishes no mode shapes, frequencies or damping. RESHAPED IN MILESTONE 15, and the shape it replaced is the point. The weights used to ascend 0.25, 0.4, 0.9, 3.0, 7.0 and 12.0 - a span of 16.8 dB rising with frequency - to compensate for the premixed Wiebe rise starting with zero slope and so driving the upper modes weakly. That compensation was overdone and it was audible: a listener reported too much high frequency from this path, and the same reshape answered a second report, because ascending weights starved the 220-750 Hz band a diesel growls in. The bank now spans 6.7 dB and rises gently. Measured, the block path went from 22.6% to 49.8% of its energy in the first four firing orders at cruise, and its loudest octave moved to 315-630 Hz.
provenance.purpose: Where the block, head and covers ring, which is what turns the pressure trace into combustion noise rather than into a tone. The frequencies place the mechanism, the Q values set how long each rings, and the weights set the shape of the path. Q is lowest at 750 and 1400 Hz, where the two heaviest weights sit, and that is deliberate: a shorter ring is a more transient one, and it is what keeps the mix crest factor above its 9 dB floor at rated speed. The block supplies crest - its own is around 13 dB - so quieting it to hold the exhaust-over-block balance costs the mix crest, and low Q buys it back.

provenance.value_note: 0.09. Calibrated against the audio_probe path balance so the exhaust leads the body by roughly 2 to 11 dB across the operating range, the spread being physical rather than sloppy: torque fluctuation grows with load faster than port flow does. The ceiling is set by where the energy lands, not by taste - at 0.4 the body path alone carried three quarters of the total output below 80 Hz, which measures as a magnificent low end and is inaudible on a laptop speaker and on in-ear monitors alike. The source manual publishes nothing about this.
provenance.purpose: Sets the level of the torque-driven body path against the exhaust path. This is the path that carries the roar: the engine reacting against its mounts, shaking the frame and cab panels between roughly 20 and 200 Hz. It is not a variation on the structural path and cannot be replaced by one, because it is driven by a different quantity - crank torque swings through the whole cycle at the firing frequency and its low orders, while cylinder pressure spikes once per cycle with a fast premixed edge and drives the hundreds-of-hertz modes. Too low and a 12.8 litre six sounds like a much smaller engine; too high and the output is dominated by content below 80 Hz, which is headroom spent where no ordinary speaker reproduces anything.

provenance.value_note: Four modes at 60, 95, 150 and 220 Hz with Q of 4.0, 4.0, 4.5 and 5.0, weighted 1.0, 1.0, 0.8 and 0.5. Plausible for the frame and cab panels of a vehicle of this class and nothing more than that: the source manual is an engine manual and publishes nothing about the vehicle, let alone about its structural modes. Placed to straddle the firing frequency across the whole speed range - an inline six runs 28 Hz at idle to about 105 Hz governed - so the roar follows engine speed with nothing scheduling it. Four modes rather than three, and Q in the single figures rather than the tens, because a sparser or sharper bank made the path's level jump by 6 dB between operating points purely on whether the firing frequency happened to land on a mode.
provenance.purpose: The modal bank the fluctuating crank torque shakes through the engine mounts. Each mode is one two-pole resonator standing for a frame or cab panel resonance. The Q values are deliberately far lower than the structural bank's: a panel on a trimmed cab is heavily damped, and a sharp bank here would be a tonal drone that jumped in level as the firing frequency swept past each mode rather than a roar that tracks engine speed smoothly. Pole radius 1 - pi f dt / Q must stay inside (0, 1) or the mode is unstable, and validation rejects that rather than letting it grow in the hot loop.

provenance.value_note: 0.25, after a first attempt at 0.35 and a second at 1.1. Set against the *cranking window* of the start capture specifically - 0.10 to 0.58 s, before the engine catches - because that is the only window where the starter and the engine being turned over are both present, and the balance between those two is what a listener judges. Any average over the whole scenario is misleading: the pinion is in mesh for 0.48 s of 4 s, so a whole-capture figure is mostly idle. At 0.25 the starter leads the exhaust by 4.7 dB across that window and peaks at 0.095. At 1.1 it led by 17.6 dB, and a listener reported hearing nothing but the starter - which is exactly what the measurement says. Neither the engine manual nor the starter catalogue publishes anything about this.
provenance.purpose: Sets the level of the starter tooth-mesh path against the exhaust path. Unlike the other three gains this one is audible for half a second at a time and silent otherwise - the path emits exactly zero with the pinion retracted - so it cannot be calibrated against any steady operating point and is constrained by none of them. Too low and a start has no starter in it, which is the defect this path was added to fix; too high and it masks the engine being turned over, which is the defect the first calibration of it caused.

provenance.value_note: 210, 430, 850 and 1750 Hz at Q 4.5, 5.5, 6.0 and 7.0, weighted 1.0, 1.0, 0.55 and 0.22. Four modes rather than three, and reaching an octave and a half lower, because the structure is not only the starter: the pinion drives a ring gear bolted to the flywheel, inside a large steel housing between the block and the gearbox, and that casting rings far below 850 Hz. The first version of this bank started at 850 Hz and a listener heard the result as a screeching belt - measured, it held 94.7% of its energy between 300 Hz and 2 kHz and 2.9% below 300. Q came down with it: at 8 to 12 the bank rings long enough to sound pitched, and a starter is a rough mechanical whirr rather than a tone.
provenance.purpose: The structure the tooth-mesh force rings, and what decides whether the starter reads as heavy machinery or as a small bright motor. Too high and it screeches; too low and it disappears under the compression thump it is meant to sit over. Q is deliberately in the single figures so the whine is broadband texture across the whole cranking speed range rather than a pitch that appears only when the mesh rate sweeps past a resonance.

provenance.value_note: 375 kW for power code M3D. The engine speed at which this occurs is NOT published; the speed this model reaches it at is our calibration.
